entries.d4d2f0d8bf3b63651655a23c2682fadb2b19fefe: <div sID="gen10423" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="Ps.7" sID="Ps.7"/> <div eID="gen10423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10424" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10425" type="x-p"/> It appears by the title that this psalm was penned with a particular reference to the malicious imputations that David was unjustly laid under by some of his enemies. Being thus wronged, I. He applies to God for favour, <reference osisRef="Ps.7.1-Ps.7.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. He appeals to God concerning his innocency as to those things whereof he was accused, <reference osisRef="Ps.7.3-Ps.7.5">ver. 3-5</reference>. III. He prays to God to plead his cause and judge for him against his persecutors, <reference osisRef="Ps.7.6-Ps.7.9">ver. 6-9</reference>. IV. He expresses his confidence in God that he would do so, and would return the mischief upon the head of those that designed it against him, <reference osisRef="Ps.7.10-Ps.7.16">ver. 10-16</reference>. V. He promises to give God the glory of his deliverance, <reference osisRef="Ps.7.17">ver. 17</reference>. In this David was a type of Christ, who was himself, and still is in his members, thus injured, but will certainly be righted at last.
entries.77f3d7bf9699b9cafadceabb62c8b192f554e485: <div eID="gen10425" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10424" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">David Prays Against His Enemies; Prayer for Sinners and Saints.</title> <div sID="gen10426" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> my God, in thee do I put my trust: save me from all them that persecute me, and deliver me: <hi type="super">2</hi> Lest he tear my soul like a lion, rending <hi type="italic">it</hi> in pieces, while <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none to deliver. <hi type="super">3</hi> <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> my God, if I have done this; if there be iniquity in my hands; <hi type="super">4</hi> If I have rewarded evil unto him that was at peace with me; (yea, I have delivered him that without cause is mine enemy:) <hi type="super">5</hi> Let the enemy persecute my soul, and take <hi type="italic">it;</hi> yea, let him tread down my life upon the earth, and lay mine honour in the dust. Selah. <hi type="super">6</hi> Arise, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , in thine anger, lift up thyself because of the rage of mine enemies: and awake for me <hi type="italic">to</hi> the judgment <hi type="italic">that</hi> thou hast commanded. <hi type="super">7</hi> So shall the congregation of the people compass thee about: for their sakes therefore return thou on high. <hi type="super">8</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall judge the people: judge me, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , according to my righteousness, and according to mine integrity <hi type="italic">that is</hi> in me. <hi type="super">9</hi> Oh let the wickedness of the wicked come to an end; but establish the just: for the righteous God trieth the hearts and reins. <div eID="gen10426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10427" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Shiggaion</hi> is a <hi type="italic">song</hi> or <hi type="italic">psalm</hi> (the word is used so only here and <reference osisRef="Hab.3.1">Hab. iii. 1</reference>)—a <hi type="italic">wandering</hi> song (so some), the matter and composition of the several parts being different, but artificially put together—a <hi type="italic">charming</hi> song (so others), very delightful. David not only penned it, but sang it himself in a devout religious manner unto the Lord, <hi type="italic">concerning the words</hi> or affairs <hi type="italic">of Cush the Benjamite,</hi> that is, of Saul himself, whose barbarous usage of David bespoke him rather a Cushite, or Ethiopian, than a true-born Israelite. Or, more likely, it was some kinsman of Saul named <hi type="italic">Cush,</hi> who was an inveterate enemy to David, misrepresented him to Saul as a traitor, and (which was very needless) exasperated Saul against him, one of those children of men, children of Belial indeed, whom David complains of (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.19">1 Sam. xxvi. 19</reference>), that made mischief between him and Saul. David, thus basely abused, has recourse to the Lord. The injuries men do us should drive us to God, for to him we may commit our cause. Nay, he sings to the Lord; his spirit was not ruffled by it, nor cast down, but so composed and cheerful that he was still in tune for sacred songs and it did not occasion one jarring string in his harp. Thus let the injuries we receive from men, instead of provoking our passions, kindle and excite our devotions. In <reference osisRef="Ps.7.1-Ps.7.9">these verses</reference>, <div eID="gen10427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10428" type="x-p"/> I. He puts himself under God's protection and flies to him for succour and shelter (<reference osisRef="Ps.7.1">v. 1</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Lord, save me, and deliver me</hi> from the power and malice of <hi type="italic">all those that persecute me,</hi> that they may not have their will against me." He pleads, 1. His relation to God. "Thou art <hi type="italic">my God,</hi> and therefore whither else should I go but to thee? Thou art my God, and therefore my shield (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.1">Gen. xv. 1</reference>), my God, and therefore I am one of thy servants, who may expect to be protected." 2. His confidence in God: "Lord, save me, for I depend upon thee: <hi type="italic">In thee do I put my trust,</hi> and not in any arm of flesh." Men of honour will not fail those that repose a trust in them, especially if they themselves have encouraged them to do so, which is our case. 3. The rage and malice of his enemies, and the imminent danger he was in of being swallowed up by them: "Lord, save me, or I am gone; he will <hi type="italic">tear my soul like a lion</hi> tearing his prey," with so much pride, and pleasure, and power, so easily, so cruelly. St. Paul compares Nero to a lion (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.17">2 Tim. iv. 17</reference>), as David here compares Saul. 4. The failure of all other helpers: "Lord, be thou pleased to deliver me, for otherwise <hi type="italic">there is none to deliver,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.7.2">v. 2</reference>. It is the glory of God to help the helpless. <div eID="gen10428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10429" type="x-p"/> II. He makes a solemn protestation of his innocency as to those things whereof he was accused, and by a dreadful imprecation appeals to God, the searcher of hearts, concerning it, <reference osisRef="Ps.7.3-Ps.7.5">v. 3-5</reference>. Observe, in general, 1. When we are falsely accused by men it is a great comfort if our own consciences acquit us— <div eID="gen10429" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen10430"/> <l level="1" sID="gen10431"/>———————- Hic murus aheneus esto,<l eID="gen10431" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen10432"/>Nil conscire sibi.———————————<l eID="gen10432" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen10433"/>Be this thy brazen bulwark of defence,<l eID="gen10433" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen10434"/>Still to preserve thy conscious innocence.—<l eID="gen10434" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen10430"/> <div sID="gen10435" type="x-p"/> III. Having this testimony of his conscience concerning his innocency, he humbly prays to God to appear for him against his persecutors, and backs every petition with a proper plea, as one that knew how to order his cause before God. <div eID="gen10435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10436" type="x-p"/> 1. He prays that God would manifest his wrath against his enemies, and pleads their wrath against him: "Lord, they are unjustly angry at me, be thou justly angry with them and let them know that thou art so, <reference osisRef="Ps.7.6">v. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">In thy anger lift up thyself</hi> to the seat of judgment, and make thy power and justice conspicuous, <hi type="italic">because of the rage,</hi> the furies, the outrages (the word is plural) <hi type="italic">of my enemies.</hi>" Those need not fear men's wrath against them who have God's wrath for them. <hi type="italic">Who knows the power of his anger?</hi> <div eID="gen10436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10437" type="x-p"/> 2. He prays that God would plead his cause. <div eID="gen10437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10438" type="x-p"/> (1.) He prays, <hi type="italic">Awake for me to judgment</hi> (that is, let my cause have a hearing), to <hi type="italic">the judgment which thou hast commanded;</hi> this speaks, [1.] The divine power; as he blesses effectually, and is therefore said to <hi type="italic">command the blessing,</hi> so he judges effectually, and is therefore said to <hi type="italic">command the judgment,</hi> which is such as none can countermand; for it certainly carries execution along with it. [2.] The divine purpose and promise: "It is the judgment which thou hast determined to pass upon all the enemies of thy people. Thou hast commanded the princes and judges of the earth to give redress to the injured and vindicate the oppressed; Lord, awaken thyself to that judgment." He that loves righteousness, and requires it in others, will no doubt execute it himself. Though he seem to connive at wrong, as one asleep, he will awake in due time (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.65">Ps. lxxviii. 65</reference>) and will make it to appear that the delays were no neglects. <div eID="gen10438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10439" type="x-p"/> (2.) He prays (<reference osisRef="Ps.7.7">v. 7</reference>), "<hi type="italic">Return thou on high,</hi> maintain thy own authority, resume thy royal throne of which they have despised the sovereignty, and the judgment-seat of which they have despised the sentence. Return on high, that is, visibly and in the sight of all, that it may be universally acknowledged that heaven itself owns and pleads David's cause." Some make this to point at the resurrection and ascension of Jesus Christ, who, when he returned to heaven (returned on high in his exalted state), had all judgment committed to him. Or it may refer to his second coming, when he shall return on high to this world, to execute judgment upon all. This return his injured people wait for, and pray for, and to it they appeal from the unjust censures of men. <div eID="gen10439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10440" type="x-p"/> (3.) He prays again (<reference osisRef="Ps.7.8">v. 8</reference>), "<hi type="italic">Judge me,</hi> judge for me, give sentence on my side." To enforce this suit, [1.] He pleads that his cause was now brought into the proper court: <hi type="italic">The Lord shall judge the people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.7.8">v. 8</reference>. He is the Judge of all the earth, and therefore no doubt he will do right and all will be obliged to acquiesce in his judgment. [2.] He insists upon his integrity as to all the matters in variance between him and Saul, and desires only to be judged, in this matter, according to his righteousness, and the sincerity of his heart in all the steps he had taken towards his preferment. [3.] He foretels that it would be much for the glory of God and the edification and comfort of his people if God would appear for him: "<hi type="italic">So shall the congregation of the people compass thee about;</hi> therefore do it for their sakes, that they may attend thee with their raises and services in the courts of thy house." <hi type="italic">First,</hi> They will do it of their own accord. God's appearing on David's behalf, and fulfilling his promise to him, would be such an instance of his righteousness, goodness, and faithfulness, as would greatly enlarge the hearts of all his faithful worshippers and fill their mouths with praise. David was the darling of his country, especially of all the good people in it; and therefore, when they saw him in a fair way to the throne, they would greatly rejoice and give thanks to God; crowds of them would attend his footstool with their praises for such a blessing to their land. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> If David come into power, as God has promised him, he will take care to bring people to church by his influence upon them, and the ark shall not be neglected, as it was <hi type="italic">in the days of Saul,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.13.3">1 Chron. xiii. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen10440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10441" type="x-p"/> 3. He prays, in general, for the conversion of sinners and the establishment of saints (<reference osisRef="Ps.7.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">O let the wickedness,</hi> not only of my wicked enemies, but <hi type="italic">of all the wicked, come to an end! but establish the just.</hi>" Here are two things which everyone of us must desire and may hope for:—(1.) The destruction of sin, that it may be brought to an end in ourselves and others. When corruption is mortified, when every wicked way and thought are forsaken, and the stream which ran violently towards the world and the flesh is driven back and runs towards God and heaven, then the wickedness of the wicked comes to an end. When there is a general reformation of manners, when atheists and profane are convinced and converted, when a stop is put to the spreading of the infection of sin, so that evil men proceed no further, their folly being made manifest, when the wicked designs of the church's enemies are baffled, and their power is broken, and the man of sin is destroyed, then the <hi type="italic">wickedness of the wicked comes to an end.</hi> And this is that which all that love God, and for his sake hate evil, desire and pray for. (2.) The perpetuity of righteousness: <hi type="italic">But establish the just.</hi> As we pray that the bad maybe made good, so we pray that the good may be made better, that they may not be seduced by the wiles of the wicked nor shocked by their malice, that they may be confirmed in their choice of the ways of God and in their resolution to persevere therein, may be firm to the interests of God and religion and zealous in their endeavours to bring <hi type="italic">the wickedness of the wicked to an end.</hi> His plea to enforce this petition is, <hi type="italic">For the righteous God trieth the hearts and the reins;</hi> and therefore he knows the secret wickedness of the wicked and knows how to bring it to an end, and the secret sincerity of the just he is witness to and has secret ways of establishing. <div eID="gen10441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10442" type="x-p"/> As far as we have the testimony of an unbiased conscience for us that in any instance we are wronged and injuriously reflected on, we may, in singing <reference osisRef="Ps.7.1-Ps.7.9">these verses</reference>, lodge our appeal with the righteous God, and be assured that he will own our righteous cause, and will one day, in the last day at furthest, bring forth our integrity as the light.
entries.9d74149df357bed10c140008b4b610aaedcb30ee: <div eID="gen10442" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Persecutor's Doom.</title> <div sID="gen10443" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> My defence <hi type="italic">is</hi> of God, which saveth the upright in heart. <hi type="super">11</hi> God judgeth the righteous, and God is angry <hi type="italic">with the wicked</hi> every day. <hi type="super">12</hi> If he turn not, he will whet his sword; he hath bent his bow, and made it ready. 13 He hath also prepared for him the instruments of death; he ordaineth his arrows against the persecutors. <hi type="super">14</hi> Behold, he travaileth with iniquity, and hath conceived mischief, and brought forth falsehood. <hi type="super">15</hi> He made a pit, and digged it, and is fallen into the ditch <hi type="italic">which</hi> he made. <hi type="super">16</hi> His mischief shall return upon his own head, and his violent dealing shall come down upon his own pate. <hi type="super">17</hi> I will praise the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> according to his righteousness: and will sing praise to the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> most high. <div eID="gen10443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10444" type="x-p"/> David having lodged his appeal with God by prayer and a solemn profession of his integrity, in the former part of the psalm, in this latter part does, as it were, take out judgment upon the appeal, by faith in the word of God, and the assurance it gives of the happiness and safety of the righteous and the certain destruction of wicked people that continue impenitent. <div eID="gen10444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10445" type="x-p"/> I. David is confident that he shall find God his powerful protector and Saviour, and the patron of his oppressed innocency (<reference osisRef="Ps.7.10">v. 10</reference>): "<hi type="italic">My defence is of God.</hi> Not only, God is my defender, and I shall find him so; but I look for defence and safety in no other; my hope for shelter in a time of danger is placed in God alone; if I have defence, it must be of God." <hi type="italic">My shield is upon God</hi> (so some read it); there is that in God which gives an assurance of protection to all that are his. His name is a strong tower, <reference osisRef="Prov.18.10">Prov. xviii. 10</reference>. Two things David builds this confidence upon:—1. The particular favour God has for all that are sincere: <hi type="italic">He saves the upright in heart,</hi> saves them with an everlasting salvation, and therefore will <hi type="italic">preserve them to his heavenly kingdom;</hi> he saves them out of their present troubles, as far as is good for them; their integrity and uprightness will preserve them. The upright in heart are safe, and ought to think themselves so, under the divine protection. 2. The general respect he has for justice and equity: <hi type="italic">God judgeth the righteous;</hi> he owns every righteous cause, and will maintain it in every righteous man, and will protect him. <hi type="italic">God is a righteous Judge</hi> (so some read it), who not only doeth righteousness himself, but will take care that righteousness be done by the children of men and will avenge and punish all unrighteousness. <div eID="gen10445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10446" type="x-p"/> II. He is no less confident of the destruction of all his persecutors, even as many of them as would not <hi type="italic">repent, to give glory to God.</hi> He reads their doom here, for their good, if possible, that they might cease from their enmity, or, however, for his own comfort, that he might not be afraid of them nor aggrieved at their prosperity and success for a time. He goes into the sanctuary of God, and there understands, <div eID="gen10446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10447" type="x-p"/> 1. That they are children of wrath. They are not to be envied, for God is angry with them, is <hi type="italic">angry with the wicked every day.</hi> They are every day doing that which is provoking to him, and he resents it, and treasures it up <hi type="italic">against the day of wrath.</hi> As his mercies are new every morning towards his people, so his anger is new every morning against the wicked, upon the fresh occasions given for it by their renewed transgressions. God is angry with the wicked even in the merriest and most prosperous of their days, even in the days of their devotion; for, if they be suffered to prosper, it is in wrath; if they pray, their very prayers are an abomination. The wrath of God abides upon them (<reference osisRef="John.3.36">John iii. 36</reference>) and continual additions are made to it. <div eID="gen10447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10448" type="x-p"/> 2. That they are children of death, as all the children of wrath are, sons of perdition, marked out for ruin. See their destruction. <div eID="gen10448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10449" type="x-p"/> (1.) God will destroy them. The destruction they are reserved for is <hi type="italic">destruction from the Almighty,</hi> which ought to be a terror to every one of us, for it comes from the <hi type="italic">wrath of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.7.13-Ps.7.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. It is here intimated, [1.] That the destruction of sinners may be prevented by their conversion, for it is threatened with that proviso: <hi type="italic">If he turn not</hi> from his evil way, if he do not let fall his enmity against the people of God, then let him expect it will be his ruin; but, if he turn, it is implied that his sin shall be pardoned and all shall be well. Thus even the threatenings of wrath are introduced with a gracious implication of mercy, enough to justify God for ever in the destruction of those that perish; they might have turned and lived, but they chose rather to go on and die and their blood is therefore upon their own heads. [2.] That, if it be not thus prevented by the conversion of the sinner, it will be prepared for him by the justice of God. In general (<reference osisRef="Ps.7.13">v. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">He has prepared for him the instruments of death,</hi> of all that death which is the wages of sin. If God will slay, he will not want instruments of death for any creature; even the least and weakest may be made so when he pleases. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Here is variety of instruments, all which breathe threatenings and slaughter. Here is a sword, which wounds and kills at hand, a bow and arrows, which wound and kill at a distance those who think to get out of the reach of God's vindictive justice. If the sinner <hi type="italic">flees from the iron weapon,</hi> yet the <hi type="italic">bow of steel shall strike him through,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.20.24">Job xx. 24</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> These instruments of death are all said to be made ready. God has them not to seek, but always at hand. <hi type="italic">Judgments are prepared for scorners. Tophet is prepared of old. Thirdly,</hi> While God is preparing his instruments of death, he gives the sinners timely warning of their danger, and space to repent and prevent it. He is slow to punish, and <hi type="italic">long-suffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish. Fourthly,</hi> The longer the destruction is delayed, to give time for repentance, the sorer will it be and the heavier will it fall and lie for ever if that time be not so improved; while God is waiting the sword is in the whetting and the bow in the drawing. <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> The destruction of impenitent sinners, though it come slowly, yet comes surely; for it is <hi type="italic">ordained,</hi> they are of old ordained to it. <hi type="italic">Sixthly,</hi> Of all sinners persecutors are set up as the fairest marks of divine wrath; against them, more than any other, God has ordained his arrows. They set God at defiance, but cannot set themselves out of the reach of his judgments. <div eID="gen10449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10450" type="x-p"/> (2.) They will destroy themselves, <reference osisRef="Ps.7.14-Ps.7.16">v. 14-16</reference>. The sinner is here described as taking a great deal of pains to ruin himself, more pains to damn his soul than, if directed aright, would save it. His conduct is described, [1.] By the pains of a labouring woman that brings forth a false conception, <reference osisRef="Ps.7.14">v. 14</reference>. The sinner's head with its politics <hi type="italic">conceives mischief,</hi> contrives it with a great deal of art, lays the plot deep, and keeps it close; the sinner's heart with its passions <hi type="italic">travails with iniquity,</hi> and is in pain to be delivered of the malicious projects it is hatching against the people of God. But what does it come to when it comes to the birth? It is falsehood; it is a cheat upon himself; it is a lie in his right hand. He cannot compass what he intended, nor, if he gain his point, will he gain the satisfaction he promised himself. He brings forth <hi type="italic">wind</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.18">Isa. xxvi. 18</reference>), <hi type="italic">stubble</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.11">Isa. xxxiii. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">death</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.5">James i. 15</reference>), that is, <hi type="italic">falsehood.</hi> [2.] By the pains of a labouring man that works hard to dig a pit, and then falls into it and perishes in it. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> This is true, in a sense of all sinners. They prepare destruction for themselves by preparing themselves for destruction, loading themselves with guilt and submitting themselves to their corruptions. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is often remarkably true of those who contrive mischief against the people of God or against their neighbours; by the righteous hand of God it is made to <hi type="italic">return upon their own heads.</hi> What they designed for the shame and destruction of others proves to be their own confusion. <div eID="gen10450" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen10451"/> <l level="1" sID="gen10452"/>——————————- Nec lex est jusitior ulla<l eID="gen10452" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen10453"/>Quam necis artifices arte perire sua————-<l eID="gen10453" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen10454"/>There is not a juster law than that the author<l eID="gen10454" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen10455"/>of a murderous contrivance shall perish by it.<l eID="gen10455" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen10451"/> <div sID="gen10456" type="x-p"/> In singing this psalm we must do as David here does (<reference osisRef="Ps.7.17">v. 17</reference>), <hi type="italic">praise the Lord according to his righteousness,</hi> that is, give him the glory of that gracious protection under which he takes his afflicted people and of that just vengeance with which he will pursue those that afflict them. Thus we must sing to the praise of the Lord most high, who, when his enemies deal proudly, shows that he is above them.  <chapter eID="Ps.7"/> <div eID="gen10456" type="x-p"/>

entries.040c9cab26d82bba20d631531bf673b78aa5df3a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5509"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 7</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.7.1-Ps.7.17">Psa 7:1-17</reference>. Shiggaion--a plaintive song or elegy. Though obscure in details, this title seems to intimate that the occasion of this Psalm was some event in David's persecution by Saul. He prays for relief because he is innocent, and God will be glorified in his vindication. He thus passes to the celebration of God's righteous government, in defending the upright and punishing the wicked, whose malignant devices will result in their own ruin; and, confident of God's aid, he closes with rejoicing.</title> <div sID="gen8361" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5509"/>1-2. Though many enemies set upon him, one is singled out as prominent, and compared to a wild beast tearing his prey to pieces (compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.1">1Sa 20:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.23">23:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.19">26:19</reference>). <div eID="gen8361" type="x-p"/>

entries.1f60a6d88bb8c7fa79eb4b9e7acaca6476d045d3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5511"/><div sID="gen8363" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5511"/>4. This is the consequence, if such has been his conduct.<div eID="gen8365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8366" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mine honour--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="Ps.3.3">Psa 3:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.4.2">4:2</reference>)--my personal and official dignity. <div eID="gen8366" type="x-p"/>

entries.6fda533d44c6255f56851a1f7a6831977767b8fb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5514"/><div sID="gen8370" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5514"/><hi type="bold">7. compass thee--</hi>as those seeking justice.<div eID="gen8370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8371" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">return thou on high--</hi>assume the judgment seat, to be honored as a just Ruler by them. <div eID="gen8371" type="x-p"/>
entries.49c8b03078a61b4495f0764bc993cec0d3d8d7c9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5515"/><div sID="gen8372" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5515"/>8. Though not claiming innocence in general, he can confidently do so in this case, and in demanding from the Judge of all the earth a judgment, he virtually asks acquittal. <div eID="gen8372" type="x-p"/>
entries.61aef95c2f936ad3d9b56f33ba72a8b60b517723: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5516"/><div sID="gen8373" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5516"/><hi type="bold">9. the hearts and reins--</hi>the affections and motives of men, or the seat of them (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.16.7">Psa 16:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.26.2">26:2</reference>); as we use heart and bosom or breast. <div eID="gen8373" type="x-p"/>

entries.4e3ee8fc10107bdf2ec1d2b132c640a593ecae89: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5518"/><div sID="gen8375" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5518"/><hi type="bold">11. judgeth--</hi>as in <reference osisRef="Ps.7.8">Psa 7:8</reference>.<div eID="gen8375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8376" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the wicked--</hi>Though not expressed, they are implied, for they alone are left as objects of anger. <div eID="gen8376" type="x-p"/>
entries.949d7ae1784c4eba2e7a0fcf6de798defdabe62b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5519"/><div sID="gen8377" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5519"/>12-13. They are here distinctly pointed out, though by changing the person, a very common mode of speech, one is selected as a representative of wicked men generally. The military figures are of obvious meaning. <div eID="gen8377" type="x-p"/>
entries.fd30cffb86ca4162116511fd5dd49f26111858c2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5521"/><div sID="gen8379" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5521"/>14. The first clause expresses the general idea that wicked men labor to do evil, the others carry out the figure fully. <div eID="gen8379" type="x-p"/>
entries.e5d7e7e7223bf5c1425d7dbe9fe510039feee0a8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5522"/><div sID="gen8380" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5522"/>15-16. <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.17">1Sa 18:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.2">31:2</reference> illustrate the statement whether alluded to or not. These verses are expository of <reference osisRef="Ps.7.14">Psa 7:14</reference>, showing how the devices of the wicked end in disappointment, falsifying their expectations. <div eID="gen8380" type="x-p"/>
entries.82ff52a3272c8b5e69fe75edeb03d6ffab0d0f39: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5523"/><div sID="gen8381" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5523"/><hi type="bold">17. his righteousness--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.5.8">Psa 5:8</reference>). Thus illustrated in the defense of His servant and punishment of the wicked. <chapter eID="Ps.7"/>

entries.00d45242b9a610371b4092c52fd5556c8d7d2789: <div eID="gen18463" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen18464" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18465" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18465" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18464" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18466" type="x-p"/> The psalmist prays against the malice of his enemies, <reference osisRef="Psa.7.1">Psa 7:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.7.2">Psa 7:2</reference>; protests his own innocence, <reference osisRef="Psa.7.3-Psa.7.5">Psa 7:3-5</reference>; prays to God that he would vindicate him, for the edification of his people, <reference osisRef="Psa.7.6-Psa.7.8">Psa 7:6-8</reference>; prays against the wickedness of his enemies, <reference osisRef="Psa.7.9">Psa 7:9</reference>; expresses strong confidence in God, <reference osisRef="Psa.7.10">Psa 7:10</reference>; threatens transgressors with God's judgments, <reference osisRef="Psa.7.11-Psa.7.13">Psa 7:11-13</reference>; shows the conduct and end of the ungodly, <reference osisRef="Psa.7.14-Psa.7.16">Psa 7:14-16</reference>; and exults in the mercy and lovingkindness of his Maker, <reference osisRef="Psa.7.17">Psa 7:17</reference>. <div eID="gen18466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18467" type="x-p"/> This Psalm is entitled, Shiggaion of David, which he sang unto the Lord, concerning the words of Cush the Benjamite. The word שגיון shiggayon comes from שגה shagah, to wander, a wandering song; i.e., a Psalm composed by David in his wanderings, when he was obliged to hide himself from the fury of Saul. <div eID="gen18467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18468" type="x-p"/> Bishop Horsley thinks it may have its name, a wandering ode, from its being in different parts, taking up different subjects, in different styles of composition. But he has sometimes thought that shiggaion might be an unpremeditated song; an improviso. <div eID="gen18468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18469" type="x-p"/> As to Cush the Benjamite, he is a person unknown in the Jewish history; the name is probably a name of disguise; and by it he may covertly mean Saul himself, the son of Kish, who was of the tribe of Benjamin. The subject of the Psalm will better answer to Saul's unjust persecution and David's innocence, than to any other subject in the history of David. <div eID="gen18469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18470" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen18470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18471" type="x-p"/> O Lord my God - יהוה אלהי Yehovah Elohai, words expressive of the strongest confidence the soul can have in the Supreme Being. Thou self-existent, incomprehensible, almighty, and eternal Being, who neither needest nor hatest any thing that thou hast made; thou art my God: God in covenant with thy creature man; and my God and portion particularly. Therefore, in thee do I put thy trust - I repose all my confidence in thee, and expect all my good from thee. <div eID="gen18471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18472" type="x-p"/> Save me - Shield me from my persecutors; abate their pride, assuage their malice, and confound their devices! <div eID="gen18472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18473" type="x-p"/> Deliver me - From the counsels which they have devised, and from the snares and gins they have laid in my path.
entries.515ee319809ecc8c2a23211e9c825917b4d73eed: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen18473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18474" type="x-p"/> Lest he tear my soul like a lion - These words seem to answer well to Saul. As the lion is king in the forest; so was Saul king over the land. As the lion, in his fierceness, seizes at once, and tears his prey in pieces; so David expected to be seized and suddenly destroyed by Saul. He had already, in his rage, thrown his javelin at him, intending to have pierced him to the wall with it. As from the power of the lion no beast in the forest could deliver any thing; so David knew that Saul's power was irresistible, and that none of his friends or well-wishers could save or deliver him out of such hands. "Lest he tear my soul (my life) like a lion, rending it in pieces, while there is none to deliver." All this answers to Saul, and to none else.
entries.616caf24d60117b7e324ecaee4518cac1eeb4400: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen18474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18475" type="x-p"/> If I have done this - David was accused by Saul of affecting the kingdom; and of waiting for an opportunity to take away the life of his king, his patron, and his friend. In his application to God he refers to these charges; meets them with indignation; and clears himself of them by a strong appeal to his Judge; and an imprecation that, if he had meditated or designed any such thing, he might meet with nothing but curse and calamity either from God or man.
entries.340ee1a30eec6fbadf59ac93dee77370ec96378d: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen18475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18476" type="x-p"/> Yea, I have delivered him - When, in the course of thy providence, thou didst put his life in my hand in the cave, I contented myself with cutting off his skirt, merely to show him the danger he had been in, and the spirit of the man whom he accused of designs against his life; and yet even for this my heart smote me, because it appeared to be an indignity offered to him who was the Lord 's anointed. This fact, and my venturing my life frequently for his good and the safety of the state, sufficiently show the falsity of such accusations, and the innocence of my life.
entries.2fd60fac802615173d99ed699410466ffa17401a: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen18476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18477" type="x-p"/> Let the enemy persecute my soul - If I have been guilty of the things laid to my charge, let the worst evils fall upon me.
entries.5223bf3b05032cd3d0d5bb514e6f4d9447532839: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen18477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18478" type="x-p"/> Arise, O Lord, in thine anger - To thee I commit my cause; arise, and sit on the throne of thy judgment in my behalf.
entries.d1674a5264567fdb7b71720c10b605af6f07e03c: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen18478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18479" type="x-p"/> For their sakes therefore return thou on high - Thy own people who compass thy altar, the faithful of the land, are full of gloomy apprehensions. They hear the charges against me; and see how I am persecuted. Their minds are divided; they know not what to think. For their sakes, return thou on high - ascend the judgment-seat; and let them see, by the dispensations of thy providence, who is innocent and who is guilty. David feared not to make this appeal to God; for the consciousness of his innocence showed him at once how the discrimination would be made.
entries.e85fca8632274a9b84216d934d0d5199a82bc0af: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen18479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18480" type="x-p"/> The Lord shall judge the people - He will execute justice and maintain truth among them. They shall not be as sheep without a shepherd. <div eID="gen18480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18481" type="x-p"/> Judge me, O Lord - Let my innocence be brought to the light, and my just dealing made clear as the noonday.
entries.ff5894f757cf4e21a7e99e8291a335288a759fc3: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen18481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18482" type="x-p"/> The wickedness of the wicked - The iniquity of Saul's conduct. <div eID="gen18482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18483" type="x-p"/> But establish the just - Show the people my uprightness.
entries.f677745a9e4f5525cc85acbdc86f052cbe695253: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen18483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18484" type="x-p"/> My defense is of God - I now leave my cause in the hands of my Judge. I have no uneasy or fearful apprehensions, because I know God will save the upright in heart.
entries.1971ee518d78a9dc680ff8a79a75adf28207ccfb: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen18484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18485" type="x-p"/> God is angry with the wicked every day - The Hebrew for this sentence is the following: ועל זעם בכל יום veel zoem becol yom; which, according to the points, is, And God is angry every day. Our translation seems to have been borrowed from the Chaldee, where the whole verse is as follows: אלהא דינא זכאה ובתקוף רגיז אל רשיעי כל יומא elaha daiyana zaccaah ubithkoph rageiz al reshiey col yoma: "God is a righteous Judge; and in strength he is angry against the wicked every day." <div eID="gen18485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18486" type="x-p"/> The Vulgate: Deus Judex justus, fortis, et patiens; numquid irascitur per sinpulos dies? "God is a Judge righteous, strong, and patient; will he be angry every day?" <div eID="gen18486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18487" type="x-p"/> The Septuagint: Ὁ Θεος Κριτης δικαιος, και ισχυρος, και μακροθυμος, μη οργην επαγων καθ' ἑκαστην ἡμεραν; "God is a righteous Judge, strong and longsuffering; not bringing forth his anger every day." <div eID="gen18487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18488" type="x-p"/> Syriac: "God is the Judge of righteousness; he is not angry every day." <div eID="gen18488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18489" type="x-p"/> The Arabic is the same as the Septuagint. <div eID="gen18489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18490" type="x-p"/> The Aethiopic: "God is a just Judge, and strong and longsuffering; he will not bring forth tribulation daily." <div eID="gen18490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18491" type="x-p"/> Coverdale: God is a righteous judge, and Gob is ever threateninge. <div eID="gen18491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18492" type="x-p"/> King Edward's Bible by Becke 1549, follows this reading. <div eID="gen18492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18493" type="x-p"/> Cardmarden: God is a righteous judge, [strong and patient] and God is provoked every day. Cardmarden has borrowed strong and patient from the Vulgate or Septuagint, but as he found nothing in the Hebrew to express them, he put the words in a smaller letter, and included them in brackets. This is followed by the prose version in our Prayer Book. <div eID="gen18493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18494" type="x-p"/> The Genevan version, printed by Barker, the king's printer, 1615, translates thus: "God judgeth the righteous, and him that contemneth God every day." On which there is this marginal note: "He doth continually call the wicked to repentance, by some signs of his judgments." My ancient Scotico - English MS. Psalter only begins with the conclusion of this Psalm. <div eID="gen18494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18495" type="x-p"/> I have judged it of consequence to trace this verse through all the ancient versions in order to be able to ascertain what is the true reading, where the evidence on one side amounts to a positive affirmation, "God is angry every day;" and, on the other side, to as positive a negation, "He is Not angry every day." The mass of evidence supports the latter reading. The Chaldee first corrupted the text by making the addition, with the wicked, which our translators have followed, though they have put the words into italics, as not being in the Hebrew text. In the MSS. collated by Kennicott and De Rossi there is no various reading on this text. <div eID="gen18495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18496" type="x-p"/> The true sense may be restored thus: - אל el, with the vowel point tsere, signifies God: אל al, the same letters, with the point pathach, signifies not. Several of the versions have read it in this way: "God judgeth the righteous, and is Not angry every day." He is not always chiding, nor is he daily punishing, notwithstanding the continual wickedness of men: hence, the ideas of patience and longsufferiny which several of the versions introduce. Were I to take any of the translations in preference to the above, I should feel most inclined to adopt that of Coverdale.
entries.68d139a021edff28a66e58f96e1d6cc7b78e4619: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen18496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18497" type="x-p"/> If he turn not - This clause the Syriac adds to the preceding verse. Most of the versions read, "If ye return not." Some contend, and not without a great show of probability, that the two verses should be read in connection, thus: "God is a just Judge; a God who is provoked every day. If (the sinner) turn not, he will whet his sword; he hath bent his bow, and made it ready." This, no doubt, gives the sense of both.
entries.f9b645ff9ab467254529bb8311f579ed2e907ded: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen18497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18498" type="x-p"/> He hath also prepared for him the instruments of death - This appears to be all a prophecy of the tragical death of Saul. He was wounded by the arrows of the Philistines; and his own keen sword, on which he fell, terminated his woful days!
entries.012a19ecd7c821c52a73c9129b7f053d97fdb68b: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen18498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18499" type="x-p"/> He travaileth with iniquity - All these terms show the pitch of envy, wrath, and malevolence, to which Saul had carried his opposition against David. He conceived mischief; he travailed with iniquity; he brought forth falsehood - all his expectations were blasted.
entries.4bee3b787317aabbcdd10d5bce941ff9456a10ba: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen18499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18500" type="x-p"/> He made a pit - He determined the destruction of David. He laid his plans with much artifice; he executed them with zeal and diligence; and when he had, as he supposed, the grave of David digged, he fell into it himself! The metaphor is taken from pits dug in the earth, and slightly covered over with reeds &c. so as not to be discerned from the solid ground; but the animal steps on them, the surface breaks, and he falls into the pit and is taken. "All the world agrees to acknowledge the equity of that sentence, which inflicts upon the guilty the punishment intended by them for the innocent." - Horne.
entries.b136c6fc5390e1e1f3ea7428afb81e40ab50e67f: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen18500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18501" type="x-p"/> Shall come down upon his own pate - Upon his scalp, קדקד kodkod, the top of the head. It may refer to knocking the criminal on the head, in order to deprive him of life. Had scalping been known in those days, I should have thought the reference might be to that barbarous custom.
entries.8f9d7a65ac5a79b5aaed5be23afb57761331f52a: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen18501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18502" type="x-p"/> I will praise the Lord according to his righteousness - I shall celebrate both his justice and his mercy. I will sing praise to the name of the Lord Most High. The name of God is often put for his perfections. So here, שם יהוה עלין shem Yehovah Elyon; "The perfections of Jehovah, who is above all." My old Scotico - English MS., mentioned at the conclusion of the introduction, begins at this verse, where are the following words by way of paraphrase: Sang falles til ioy; and he that synges well that name, his ioy es mare than i kan tell. Those who are happy may sing; and he who can duly celebrate the name of God, who knows it to be a strong tower into which he can run and find safety, has inexpressible happiness. That is the sense of the above.  <chapter eID="Ps.7"/> <div eID="gen18502" type="x-p"/>

entries.b08a30de59a96c76cc51937e91361c8530f48b9a: <div eID="gen9091" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Appeal to the Judge of the Whole Earth against Slander and Requiting Good with Evil</title> <div sID="gen9092" type="x-p"/> In the second part of <reference osisRef="Ps.6.1-Ps.6.10">Psa 6:1-10</reference> David meets his enemies with strong self-confidence in God. Ps 7, which even Hitzig ascribes to David, continues this theme and exhibits to us, in a prominent example taken from the time of persecution under Saul, his purity of conscience and joyousness of faith. One need only read 1 Sam 24-26 to see how this Psalm abounds in unmistakeable references to this portion of David’s life. The superscribed statement of the events that gave rise to its composition point to this. Such statements are found exclusively only by the Davidic Psalms.<note placement="foot">Viz. <reference osisRef="Ps.7.1">Psa 7:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.59.1">Psa 59:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.56.1">Psa 56:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.34.1">Psa 34:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.52.1">Psa 52:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.57.1">Psa 57:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.142.1">Psa 142:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.54.1">Psa 54:1</reference> (belonging to the time of the persecution under Saul), <reference osisRef="Ps.3.1">Psa 3:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.63.1">Psa 63:1</reference> (to the persecution under Absolom), <reference osisRef="Ps.51.1">Psa 51:1</reference> (David’s adultery), <reference osisRef="Ps.60.1">Psa 60:1</reference> (the Syro-Ammonitish war).</note> <div eID="gen9092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9093" type="x-p"/> The inscription runs: <hi type="italic">Shiggajon of David, which he sang to Jahve on account of the sayings of Cush a Benjamite.</hi> על־דּברי is intentionally chosen instead of על which has other functions in these superscriptions. Although דּבר and דּברי can mean a thing, business, affairs (<reference osisRef="Exod.22.8">Exo 22:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.2">1Sa 10:2</reference>, and freq.) and על־דּברי “in reference to” (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.21">Deu 4:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.7.22">Jer 7:22</reference>) or “on occasion of” (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.1">Jer 14:1</reference>), still we must here keep to the most natural signification: “on account of the words (speeches).” <hi type="italic">Cûsh</hi> (lxx falsely Χουσί = כּוּשׁי; Luther, likewise under misapprehension, “the Moor”) must have been one of the many servants of Saul, his kinsman, one of the talebearers like Doeg and the Ziphites, who shamefully slandered David before Saul, and roused him against David. The epithet בּן־ימיני (as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.1">1Sa 9:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.21">1Sa 9:21</reference>, cf. אישׁ־ימיני   <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.1">2Sa 20:1</reference>) describes him as “a Benjamite” and does not assume any knowledge of him, as would be the case if it were הבּנימיני, or rather (in accordance with biblical usage) בּן־הימיני. And this accords with the actual fact, for there is no mention of him elsewhere in Scripture history. The statement וגו על־דברי is hardly from David’s hand, but written by some one else, whether from tradition or from the דברי הימים of David, where this Psalm may have been interwoven with the history of its occasion. Whereas there is nothing against our regarding לדוד שׁגּיון, or at least שׁגיון, as a note appended by David himself. <div eID="gen9093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9094" type="x-p"/> Since שׁגּיון (after the form הזּיון a vision) belongs to the same class as superscribed appellations like מזמור and משׂכּיל, and the <hi type="italic">Tephilla</hi> of Habakkuk, <reference osisRef="Hab.3.1">Hab 3:1</reference> (vid., my <hi type="italic">Commentary</hi>), has the addition על־שׁגינות, שׁגיון must be the name of a kind of lyric composition, and in fact a kind described according to the rhythm of its language or melody. Now since שׁגה means to go astray, wander, reel, and is cognate with שׁגע (whence comes שׁגּעון madness, a word formed in the same manner) שׁגיון may mean in the language of prosody a reeling poem, i.e., one composed in a most excited movement and with a rapid change of the strongest emotions, therefore a dithyrambic poem, and שׁגינות dithyrambic rhythms, variously and violently mixed together. Thus Ewald and Rödiger understand it, and thus even Tarnov, Geier, and other old expositors who translate it <hi type="italic">cantio erratica</hi>. What we therefore look for is that this Psalm shall consist, as Ainsworth expresses it (1627), “of sundry variable and wandering verses,” that it shall wander through the most diverse rhythms as in a state of intoxication - an expectation which is in fact realized. The musical accompaniment also had its part in the general effect produced. Moreover, the contents of the Psalm corresponds to this poetic musical style. It is the most solemn pathos of exalted self-consciousness which is expressed in it. And in common with Hab it gives expression to the joy which arises from zealous anger against the enemies of God and from the contemplation of their speedy overthrow. Painful unrest, defiant self-confidence, triumphant ecstasy, calm trust, prophetic certainty-all these states of mind find expression in the irregular arrangement of the strophes of this Davidic dithyramb, the ancient customary Psalm for the feast of Purim (<hi type="italic">Sofrim</hi> xviii. §2).  <div eID="gen9094" type="x-p"/>
entries.4f69b3e431b8e11bb07ab4fd4019bcc5ac0ab778: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2"/><div sID="gen9095" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2"/><reference osisRef="Ps.7.1-Ps.7.2">Psa 7:1-2</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_7:2-3) With this word of faith, love, and hope בּך חסיתּי (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.141.8">Psa 141:8</reference>), this holy <hi type="italic">captatio benevolentiae</hi>, David also begins in <reference osisRef="Ps.11.1">Psa 11:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.16.1">Psa 16:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.2">Psa 31:2</reference>, cf. Psa 71:1. The <hi type="italic">perf</hi>. is inchoative: in Thee have I taken my refuge, equivalent to: in Thee do I trust. The transition from the multitude of his persecutors to the <hi type="italic">sing</hi>. in <reference osisRef="Ps.7.3">Psa 7:3</reference> is explained most naturally, as one looks at the inscription, thus: that of the many the one who is just at the time the worst of all comes prominently before his mind. The verb טרף from the primary signification <hi type="italic">carpere</hi> (which corresponds still more exactly to חרף) means both to tear off and to tear in pieces (whence טרפה that which is torn in pieces); and פּרק from its primary signification <hi type="italic">frangere</hi> means both to break loose and to break in pieces, therefore to liberate, e.g., in <reference osisRef="Ps.136.24">Psa 136:24</reference>, and to break in small pieces, 1Ki 19:11. The persecutors are conceived of as wild animals, as lions which rend their prey and craunch its bones. Thus blood-thirsty are they for his soul, i.e., his life. After the painful unrest of this first strophe, the second begins the tone of defiant self-consciousness.
entries.4fa16d92f59646b11c8518f2d853dddd19511cd1: <reference osisRef="Ps.7.3-Ps.7.5">Psa 7:3-5</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_7:4-6) According to the inscription זאת points to the substance of those slanderous sayings of the Benjamite. With בּכפּי אם־ישׁ־עול one may compare David’s words to Saul אין בּידי רעה   <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.12">1Sa 24:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.18">1Sa 26:18</reference>; and from this comparison one will at once see in a small compass the difference between poetical and prose expression. שׁלמי (Targ. לבעל שׁלמי) is the name he gives (with reference to Saul) to him who stands on a peaceful, friendly footing with him, cf. the adject. שׁלום, <reference osisRef="Ps.55.21">Psa 55:21</reference>, and אישׁ שׁלום, Psa 41:10. The verb גּמל, cogn. גּמר, signifies originally to finish, complete, (root גם, כם ,גם t, cf. כּימה to be or to make full, to gather into a heap). One says טּוב גּמל and גּמל רע, and also without a material object גּמל עלי or גּמלני <hi type="italic">benefecit </hi>or<hi type="italic">malefecit mihi</hi>. But we join גּמלתּי with רע according to the Targum and contrary to the accentuation, and not with שׁלמי (Olsh., Böttch., Hitz.), although שׁלם beside משׁלּם, as e.g., דּבר beside מדבּר might mean “requiting.” The poet would then have written: אם שׁלּמתּי גּמלי רע i.e., if I have retaliated upon him that hath done evil to me. In <reference osisRef="Ps.7.5">Psa 7:5</reference> we do not render it according the meaning to הלּץ which is usual elsewhere: but rather I rescued... (Louis de Dieu, Ewald §345, a, and Hupfeld). Why cannot הלּץ in accordance with its primary signification <hi type="italic">expedire, exuere</hi> (according to which even the signification of rescuing, taken exactly, does not proceed from the idea of drawing out, but of making loose, <hi type="italic">exuere vinclis</hi>) signify here <hi type="italic">exuere = spoliare,</hi> as it does in Aramaic? And how extremely appropriate it is as an allusion to the incident in the cave, when David did not rescue Saul, but, without indeed designing to take חליצה, <hi type="italic">exuviae</hi>, cut off the hem of his garment! As Hengstenberg observes, “He affirms his innocence in the most general terms, thereby showing that his conduct towards Saul was not anything exceptional, but sprang from his whole disposition and mode of action.” On the 1 <hi type="italic">pers. fut. conv</hi>. and <hi type="italic">ah</hi>, vid., on Psa 3:6. ריקם belongs to צוררי, like <reference osisRef="Ps.25.3">Psa 25:3</reference>; Psa 69:5. <div eID="gen9095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9096" type="x-p"/> In the apodosis, <reference osisRef="Ps.7.6">Psa 7:6</reference>, the <hi type="italic">fut. Kal</hi> of רדף is made into three syllables, in a way altogether without example, since, by first making the <hi type="italic">Shebâ</hi> audible, from ירדּף it is become ירדף (like יצחק <reference osisRef="Gen.21.6">Gen 21:6</reference>, תּהלך <reference osisRef="Ps.73.9">Psa 73:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.9.23">Exo 9:23</reference>, שׁמעה <reference osisRef="Ps.39.13">Psa 39:13</reference>), and this is then sharpened by an euphonic <hi type="italic">Dag. forte</hi>.<note placement="foot">The <hi type="italic">Dag</hi>. is of the same kind as the <hi type="italic">Dag</hi>. in גּמלּים among nouns; Arabic popular dialect <hi type="italic">farassı̂</hi> (my horse), vid., Wetzstein’s <hi type="italic">Inshriften</hi> S. 366.</note> <div eID="gen9096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9097" type="x-p"/> Other ways of explaining it, as that by Cahjúg = יתרדף, or by Kimchi as a mixed form from <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> and <hi type="italic">Piel</hi>,<note placement="foot">Pinsker’s view, that the pointing ירדף is designed to leave the reader at liberty to choose between the reading ירדּף and ירדּף, cannot be supported. There are no safe examples for the supposition that the variations of tradition found expression in this way.</note> have been already refuted by Baer, <hi type="italic">Thorath Emeth</hi>, p. 33. This dactylic jussive form of <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> is followed by the regular jussives of <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. ישּׂג and ישׁכּן. The rhythm is similar so that in the primary passage <reference osisRef="Exod.15.9">Exo 15:9</reference>, which also finds its echo in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.38">Psa 18:38</reference>, - viz. iambic with anapaests inspersed. By its parallelism with נפשׁי and חיּי, כּבודי acquires the signification “my soul,” as Saadia, Gecatilia and Aben-Ezra have rendered it - a signification which is secured to it by <reference osisRef="Ps.16.9">Psa 16:9</reference>; 30:13; <reference osisRef="Ps.57.9">Psa 57:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.108.2">Psa 108:2</reference>, Gen 49:6. Man’s soul is his <hi type="italic">doxa</hi>, and this it is as being the copy of the divine <hi type="italic">doxa</hi> (<hi type="italic">Bibl. Psychol</hi>. S. 98, [tr. p. 119], and frequently). Moreover, “let him lay in the dust” is at least quite as favourable to this sense of כבודי as to the sense of personal and official dignity (<reference osisRef="Ps.3.4">Psa 3:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.4.3">Psa 4:3</reference>). To lay down in the dust is equivalent to: to lay in the dust of death, Psa 22:16. שׁכני עפר, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.19">Isa 26:19</reference>, are the dead. According to the biblical conception the soul is capable of being killed (Num 35:11), and mortal (Num 23:10). It binds spirit and body together and this bond is cut asunder by death. David will submit willingly to death in case he has ever acted dishonourably. <div eID="gen9097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9098" type="x-p"/> Here the music is to strike up, in order to give intensity to the expression of this courageous confession. In the next strophe is affirmation of innocence rises to a challenging appeal to the judgment-seat of God and a prophetic certainty that that judgment is near at hand.
entries.1fee22dd8a5e615088887b55a076c381423f4476: <reference osisRef="Ps.7.6-Ps.7.8">Psa 7:6-8</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_7:7-9) In the consciousness of his own innocence he calls upon Jahve to sit in judgment and to do justice to His own. His vision widens and extends from the enemies immediately around to the whole world in its hostility towards Jahve and His anointed one. In the very same way special judgments and the judgment of the world are portrayed side by side, as it were on one canvas, in the prophets. The truth of this combination lies in the fact of the final judgment being only the finale of that judgment which is in constant execution in the world itself. The language here takes the highest and most majestic flight conceivable. By קוּמה (<hi type="italic">Milra</hi>, ass in <reference osisRef="Ps.3.8">Psa 3:8</reference>), which is one of David’s words of prayer that he has taken from the lips of Moses (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.20">Psa 9:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.10.12">Psa 10:12</reference>), he calls upon Jahve to interpose. The parallel is הנּשׂא lift Thyself up, show thyself in Thy majesty, <reference osisRef="Ps.94.2">Psa 94:2</reference>, Isa 33:10. The anger, in which He is to arise, is the principle of His judicial righteousness. With this His anger He is to gird Himself (<reference osisRef="Ps.76.11">Psa 76:11</reference>) against the ragings of the oppressors of God’s anointed one, i.e., taking vengeance on their many and manifold manifestations of hostility. עברות is a shorter form of the construct (instead of עברות <reference osisRef="Job.40.11">Job 40:11</reference>, cf. Psa 21:1-13 :31) of עברה which describes the anger as running over, breaking forth from within and passing over into words and deeds (cf. Arab. <hi type="italic">fšš ,</hi> used of water: it overflows the dam, of wrath: it breaks forth). It is contrary to the usage of the language to make משׁפּט the object to עוּרה in opposition to the accents, and it is unnatural to regard it as the accus. of direction = למּשׂפט (<reference osisRef="Ps.35.23">Psa 35:23</reference>), as Hitzig does. The accents rightly unite עוּרה אלי: awake (stir thyself) for me i.e., to help me (אלי like לקלאתי, <reference osisRef="Ps.59.5">Psa 59:5</reference>). The view, that צוּית is then precative and equivalent to צוּה: command judgment, is one that cannot be established according to syntax either here, or in Psa 71:3. It ought at least to have been וצוּית with <hi type="italic">Waw consec</hi>. On the other hand the relative rendering: Thou who hast ordered judgment (Maurer, Hengst.), is admissible, but unnecessary. We take it by itself in a confirmatory sense, not as a circumstantial clause: having commanded judgment (Ewald), but as a co-ordinate clause: Thou hast indeed enjoined the maintaining of right (Hupfeld). <div eID="gen9098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9099" type="x-p"/> The psalmist now, so to speak, arranges the judgment scene: the assembly of the nations is to form a circle round about Jahve, in the midst of which He will sit in judgment, and after the judgment He is to soar away (<reference osisRef="Gen.17.22">Gen 17:22</reference>) aloft over it and return to the heights of heaven like a victor after the battle (see <reference osisRef="Ps.68.19">Psa 68:19</reference>). Although it strikes one as strange that the termination of the judgment itself is not definitely expressed, yet the rendering of Hupfeld and others: sit Thou again upon Thy heavenly judgment-seat to judge, is to be rejected on account of the שׁוּבה (cf. on the other hand 21:14) which is not suited to it; שׁוב למּרום can only mean Jahve’s return to His rest after the execution of judgment. That which <reference osisRef="Ps.7.7">Psa 7:7</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.7.8">Psa 7:8</reference> in the boldness of faith desire, the beginning of <reference osisRef="Ps.7.9">Psa 7:9</reference> expresses as a prophetic hope, from which proceeds the prayer, that the Judge of the earth may also do justice to him (שׁפתני <hi type="italic">vindica</hi> <hi type="italic">me</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.26.1">Psa 26:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.35.24">Psa 35:24</reference>) according to his righteousness and the purity of which he is conscious, as dwelling in him. עלי is to be closely connected with תּמּי, just as one says נפשׁי עלי (<hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. S. 152 [tr. p. 180]). That which the individual as ego, distinguishes from itself as being in it, as subject, it denotes by עלי. In explaining it elliptically: “come upon me” (Ew., Olsh., Hupf.) this psychologically intelligible usage of the language is not recognised. On תּם vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.25.21">Psa 25:21</reference>; Psa 26:1.
entries.d51cb5d3d45b28db70158eace092745dc6a62a6f: <reference osisRef="Ps.7.9-Ps.7.10">Psa 7:9-10</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_7:10-11) In this strophe we hear the calm language of courageous trust, to which the rising and calmly subsiding caesural schema is particularly adapted. He is now concerned about the cessation of evil: Oh let it come to an end (גּמר intransitive as in <reference osisRef="Ps.12.2">Psa 12:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.77.9">Psa 77:9</reference>).... His prayer is therefore not directed against the individuals as such but against the wickedness that is in them. This Psalm is the key to all Psalms which contain prayers against one’s enemies. Just in the same manner וּתכונן is intended to express a wish; it is one of the comparatively rare voluntatives of the 2 <hi type="italic">pers</hi>. (Ew. §229): and mayst Thou be pleased to establish.... To the termination of evil which is desired corresponds, in a positive form of expression, the desired security and establishment of the righteous, whom it had injured and whose continuance was endangered by it. וּבחן is the beginning of a circumstantial clause, introduced by ו, but without the personal pronoun, which is not unfrequently omitted both in the leading participial clause, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.29.8">Isa 29:8</reference> (which see), and in the minor participial clause as here (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.55.20">Psa 55:20</reference>): <hi type="italic">cum sis</hi> <hi type="italic">= quoniam es</hi>. The reins are the seat of the emotions, just as the heart is the seat of the thoughts and feelings. Reins and heart lie naked before God-a description of the only kardiognoo'stees, which is repeated in <reference osisRef="Jer.11.20">Jer 11:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.20.12">Jer 20:12</reference>, Rev 2:23. In the thesis the adjective is used with אלהים in the sing. as in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.56">Psa 78:56</reference>, cf. Ps 58:12. God is the righteous God, and by his knowledge of the inmost part He is fully capable of always showing Himself both righteous in anger and righteous in mercy according to the requirements and necessity of the case. Therefore David can courageously add על־אלהים מגנּי, my shield doth God carry; ל <reference osisRef="Ps.89.19">Psa 89:19</reference>) would signify: He has it, it (my shield) belongs to Him, על (<reference osisRef="1Chr.18.7">1Ch 18:7</reference>) signifies: He bears it, or if one takes shield in the sense of protection: He has taken my protection upon Himself, has undertaken it (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.62.8">Psa 62:8</reference>, cf. Jdg 19:20), as He is in general the Saviour of all who are devoted to Him with an upright heart, i.e., a heart sincere, guileless (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.32.1">Psa 32:1</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.7.2">Psa 7:2</reference>). צדּים is intentionally repeated at the end of the first two lines - the favourite palindrome, found more especially in Isa 40:1. And to the mixed character of this Psalm belongs the fact of its being both Elohimic and Jehovic. From the calm language of heartfelt trust in God the next strophe passes over into the language of earnest warning, which is again more excited and somewhat after the style of didactic poetry.
entries.c0e79f5ff4e523074ab9025a1c32f93721c6f768: <reference osisRef="Ps.7.11-Ps.7.13">Psa 7:11-13</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_7:12-14) If God will in the end let His wrath break forth, He will not do it without having previously given threatenings thereof every day, viz., to the ungodly, cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.66.14">Isa 66:14</reference>; Mal 1:4. He makes these feel His זעם beforehand in order to strike a wholesome terror into them. The subject of the conditional clause אם־לא ישׁוּב is any ungodly person whatever; and the subject of the principal clause, as its continuation in <reference osisRef="Ps.7.14">Psa 7:14</reference> shows, is God. If a man (any one) does not repent, then Jahve will whet His sword (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.32.41">Deu 32:41</reference>). This sense of the words accords with the connection; whereas with the rendering: “forsooth He (Elohim) will again whet His sword” (Böttch., Ew., Hupf.) ישׁוּב, which would moreover stand close by ילטושׁ (cf. e.g., <reference osisRef="Gen.30.31">Gen 30:31</reference>), is meaningless; and the אם־לא of asseveration is devoid of purpose. Judgment is being gradually prepared, as the <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. implies; but, as the <hi type="italic">perff</hi>. imply, it is also on the other hand like a bow that is already strung against the sinner with the arrow pointed towards him, so that it can be executed at any moment. כּונן of the making ready, and הכין of the aiming, are used alternately. לו, referring to the sinner, stands first by way of emphasis as in <reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen 49:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.3">1Sa 2:3</reference>, and is equivalent to אליו, Eze 4:3. “Burning” arrows are fire-arrows (זקּים, זיקות, <hi type="italic">malleoli</hi>); and God’s fire-arrows are the lightnings sent forth by Him, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.15">Psa 18:15</reference>; Zec 9:14. The <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. יפעל denotes the simultaneous charging of the arrows aimed at the sinner, with the fire of His wrath. The case illustrated by Cush is generalised: by the sword and arrows the manifold energy of the divine anger is symbolised, and it is only the divine forbearance that prevents it from immediately breaking forth. The conception is not coarsely material, but the vividness of the idea of itself suggests the form of its embodiment.
entries.82e064ad742318426a2c04e9f93b521f74ab4c1d: <reference osisRef="Ps.7.14-Ps.7.17">Psa 7:14-17</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_7:15-18) This closing strophe foretells to the enemy of God, as if dictated by the judge, what awaits him; and concludes with a prospect of thanksgiving and praise. Man brings forth what he has conceived, he reaps what he has sown. Starting from this primary passage, we find the punishment which sin brings with it frequently represented under these figures of הדה and ילד (הוליד, חבּל, חיל), זרע and קצר, and first of all in Job 15:35. The act, guilt, and punishment of sin appear in general as notions that run into one another. David sees in the sin of his enemies their self-destruction. It is singular, that travail is first spoken of, and then only afterwards pregnancy. For חבּל signifies, as in Sol 8:5, ὠδίνειν, not: to conceive (Hitz.). The Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥabila</hi> (synonym of <hi type="italic">ḥamala</hi>) is not to conceive in distinction from being pregnant, but it is both: to be and to become pregnant. The accentuation indicates the correct relationship of the three members of the sentence. First of all comes the general statement: Behold he shall travail with, i.e., bring forth with writhing as in the pains of labour, און, evil, as the result which proceeds from his wickedness. Then, by this thought being divided into its two factors (Hupf.) it goes on to say: that is, he shall conceive (<hi type="italic">concipere</hi>) עמל, and bear שׁקר. The former signifies trouble, <hi type="italic">molestia</hi>, just as πονηρία signifies that which makes πόνον; the latter falsehood, viz., self-deception, delusion, vanity, inasmuch as the burden prepared for others, returns as a heavy and oppressive burden upon the sinner himself, as is said in <reference osisRef="Ps.7.17">Psa 7:17</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.59.4">Isa 59:4</reference>, where און instead of שׁקר denotes the accursed wages of sin which consist in the unmasking of its nothingness, and in the undeceiving of its self-delusion. He diggeth a pit for himself, is another turn of the same thought, <reference osisRef="Ps.57.7">Psa 57:7</reference>; Ecc 10:8. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.7.16">Psa 7:16</reference></hi> mentions the digging, and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.7.16">Psa 7:16</reference></hi> the subsequent falling into the pit; the aorist ויּפּל is, for instance, like <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.7.13">Psa 7:13</reference></hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.16.9">Psa 16:9</reference>; Psa 29:10. The attributive יפעל is virtually a genitive to שׁחת, and is rightly taken by Ges. §124, 3, <hi type="italic">a</hi> as present: in the midst of the execution of the work of destruction prepared for others it becomes his own. The trouble, עמל, prepared for others returns upon his own head (בּראשׁו, clinging to it, just as על־ראשׁו signifies descending and resting upon it), and the violence, חמס, done to others, being turned back by the Judge who dwells above (Mic 1:12), descends upon his own pate (קדקדו with <hi type="italic">o</hi> by <hi type="italic">q,</hi> as e.g., in <reference osisRef="Gen.2.23">Gen 2:23</reference>). Thus is the righteousness of God revealed in wrath upon the oppressor and in mercy upon him who is innocently oppressed. Then will the rescued one, then will David, give thanks unto Jahve, as is due to Him after the revelation of His righteousness, and will sing of the name of Jahve the Most High (עליון as an appended name of God is always used without the <hi type="italic">art</hi>., e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.57.3">Psa 57:3</reference>). In the revelation of Himself He has made Himself a name. He has, however, revealed Himself as the almighty Judge and Deliverer, as the God of salvation, who rules over everything that takes place here below. It is this name, which He has made by His acts, that David will then echo back to Him in his song of thanksgiving.  <chapter eID="Ps.7"/> <div eID="gen9099" type="x-p"/>
